The memory cost of the parent pointer (HW2 Mutation 3): our O(1)-space `rb_foreach` walks parent pointers, so the spec asks what that pointer costs. There are three different numbers here, and they shouldn't be confused. The structure size is the first one: measured with `sizeof` on this toolchain (gcc 15.2, x86-64), `struct rb_node` is 48 bytes with the parent pointer and 40 bytes without it. The pool stride is the second: the pool rounds every slot up to `alignof(max_align_t)`, which is 16 bytes here, so both 48 and 40 round to the same 48-byte stride, and a 4096-byte slab holds 85 nodes either way (measured with `rb_pool_geometry`). In pooled mode the parent pointer therefore costs nothing extra right now, but that is an accident of the current layout and alignment, not something the design guarantees. The third number is heap allocation overhead, which depends on the allocator implementation rather than on our code: in ordinary mode each node is its own `malloc`, and glibc 2.43 reported a usable size of 56 bytes for the 48-byte node and 40 bytes for the 40-byte one. Since glibc's per-chunk header is the same in both cases, the pointer costs 16 bytes per node there, and another allocator could round differently. Key copies are separate allocations and aren't affected. `pool_stats` counts objects, not bytes, and the pool's object size is `sizeof(struct rb_node)`, which already includes the pointer, so no change was needed there. We kept the pointer because it was already there since HW1 (deletion fixup depends on it) and because the alternative, Morris traversal, writes into the tree during a read-only walk.

Stress-test sizes: the spec's million-node requirement is met under AddressSanitizer/UBSan, not under valgrind. `make stress-asan` runs `test_rbtree --stress 1000000`, which builds a 10^6-node tree, balanced and as a single left spine, in both heap and pooled mode, and runs `rb_foreach` and then `rb_destroy` on a thread with a 64 KB stack. Valgrind is many times slower, so `make memcheck` routinely runs the same harness at 20,000 nodes (`--stress 20000`), and `make test`/`make asan` run that 20,000-node size too. This is a deliberate shrink for runtime, made so `make memcheck` still finishes quickly, and it is only for valgrind. The full million-node case is never skipped; it lives behind its own target. The 20,000-node size is still big enough to catch recursion: the recursive `rb_foreach` overflowed the 64 KB stack on the 20,000-node left spine and AddressSanitizer reported it as a stack overflow in `foreach_inorder`.
EOF

lines: DECIDED: (1) **Parent pointers, not Morris.** Morris threading writes temporary `right` links into nodes reached through a `const rbtree_t *`. While a thread is in place, a callback's `rb_find` for an absent key between a threaded node and its successor follows the thread back down and loops forever; a callback that longjmps or exits strands the threads and leaves the tree corrupt; and every pass would write into slab memory. The parent pointer has existed since HW1 and `delete_fixup` already depends on it, so the walk adds no new trust. (2) **Callback contract** (also NOTES.md): read-only calls on the same tree are allowed, including nested traversal; `rb_insert`/`rb_delete`/`rb_destroy` on the traversed tree are undefined behaviour, with no "safe subset" promised — the successor is computed from `cur` after `fn` returns, and a two-children delete frees the *successor's* node, so even reading the successor first would not help. A callback that never returns leaves the tree valid, as a consequence of a walk that never writes, not as an extra promise. No NULL-tolerance or thread-safety claims beyond the header. (3) **No `pool_stats` change for the parent pointer's cost**: `obj_size` is `sizeof(struct rb_node)`, which already includes it, and the pool counts objects, not bytes; the byte cost is accounted for in REFLECTION.md.

LEARNED: First, the spec's "callbacks that call back in" question decided the algorithm, not just the contract: the in-between `rb_find` is exactly the read-only call Morris cannot survive, so it became a test (T2) rather than a remark. Second, the tests worth writing first were not the ones that turned red. T0–T2 were green against the recursive code and I said so rather than calling them red tests; the single discriminating test was the stress case already built in Evening 7, which is why its red run was captured verbatim. Third, an exact count is worth measuring even when the asymptotics are obvious: 2(n − 1) was wrong by one, and only the measurement showed it.

NEXT FIRST STEP: the fresh-context adversarial review of the HW2 work (`db085a2..HEAD` plus `src/pool.c`), run after `/clear`, with a prompt that lists areas to hunt — UAF masked by pooled slot reuse, slab-carving off-by-one, free-list link alignment, `pool_destroy` with live objects, ownership and teardown failure paths — and that does not tell the reviewer in advance what to dismiss. Triage afterwards; record one real finding and one false positive in PROMPTLOG.md only from what the review actually returns.

What surprised me the most as a C newcomer was how pointers worked, while they look simple given they're literally just a -> or a *. It took a while to learn how they really work. I also liked how the syntax isn't too different from Java. I didn't know how important it was nor how memory management worked. I had to understand that it wasn't as easy as just calling free(). I had to find out how to properly have a single stage of freeing in order to avoid a double free or use-after-free. I also had to find out that sometimes it would be simple, such as freely removing red node children.

-The memory cost of the parent pointer (HW2 Mutation 3): our O(1)-space `rb_foreach` walks parent pointers, so the spec asks what that pointer costs. There are three different numbers here, and they shouldn't be confused. The structure size is the first one: measured with `sizeof` on this toolchain (gcc 15.2, x86-64), `struct rb_node` is 48 bytes with the parent pointer and 40 bytes without it. The pool stride is the second: the pool rounds every slot up to `alignof(max_align_t)`, which is 16 bytes here, so both 48 and 40 round to the same 48-byte stride, and a 4096-byte slab holds 85 nodes either way (measured with `rb_pool_geometry`). In pooled mode the parent pointer therefore costs nothing extra right now, but that is an accident of the current layout and alignment, not something the design guarantees. The third number is heap allocation overhead, which depends on the allocator implementation rather than on our code: in ordinary mode each node is its own `malloc`, and glibc 2.43 reported a usable size of 56 bytes for the 48-byte node and 40 bytes for the 40-byte one. Since glibc's per-chunk header is the same in both cases, the pointer costs 16 bytes per node there, and another allocator could round differently. Key copies are separate allocations and aren't affected. `pool_stats` counts objects, not bytes, and the pool's object size is `sizeof(struct rb_node)`, which already includes the pointer, so no change was needed there. We kept the pointer because it was already there since HW1 (deletion fixup depends on it) and because the alternative, Morris traversal, writes into the tree during a read-only walk.
